item.title: Air Canada crews in some European cities sent to alternative locations due to civil unrest
item.description: Air Canada flight crews who flew to several cities in Europe last week were relocated to secondary hotel locations due to civil unrest related to widespread protests, a source with knowledge on the ...
item.dc:creator: Elianna Lev
item.content:encoded: Air Canada flight crews who flew to several cities in Europe last week were relocated to secondary hotel locations due to civil unrest related to widespread protests, a source with knowledge on the situation confirmed with CTVNews.ca. Air Canada crews arriving in Paris, Nice, Lyon, Nantes and Milan between Oct. 23 and 25 were sent to different locations to avoid potential disruption of crew rest. The Air Canada Master Executive Council of the Air Line Pilots Association, Int’l (ALPA), said in an email to CTVNews.ca that they work closely with airline security teams and government contacts to monitor global threats and co-ordinate crew member safety during critical events. “With safety as our top priority, relocations are common practice in the industry whenever there is a potential safety concern or possibility for disruption to our rest,” the email said. It added that crews on layover are always told to follow the Canadian government’s travel advisory information. Air Canada spokesperson Sean Davidson did not confirm the location change, but said in an email with CTVNews.ca that safety is always the airline’s top priority. “As a global airline, we continuously monitor events worldwide, follow government guidance and conduct our own security assessments in consultation with industry partners,” he said in email. “When warranted, we may temporarily relocate crew accommodations closer to the airport to ensure the on-time operation of flights to Canada.” Protest movement spread across Europe Students in France began protesting school conditions last September. As the demonstrations grew in size, so did the issues that were being protested, including the cost of living. Protesters in Spain joined in shortly after, focusing on housing costs, along with Italy, Belgium, Albania, Austria, Greece, Ireland and Portugal. Over the weekend, more than 400,000 people across France took to the streets, and nearly 1,000 people were arrested. In Italy, hundreds of troops were sent in to monitor the protests in Rome, Milan and Turin, over the weekend. which were mostly peaceful. Many luxury boutiques in Milan’s fashion district including Omega, Tiffany and Gucci, boarded up their front windows to deter possible looters. With files from rom CTV News’ Daniel Otis and The Associated Press.

item.title: PM Carney says it’s time to move beyond Indian Act
item.description: Mark Carney says he will instruct his ministers to work with First Nations to move Canada beyond the Indian Act, which could mean reforming it or abolishing it altogether.
item.dc:creator: The Canadian Press
item.content:encoded: Prime Minister Mark Carney says he will instruct his ministers to work with First Nations to move Canada beyond the Indian Act — which he said could mean reforming it or abolishing it altogether. Speaking to reporters after a meeting with First Nations chiefs and premiers in Ottawa today, Carney said the elimination of the Indian Act has been sought by many First Nations leaders, including Manitoba Premier Wab Kinew. Earlier in the day, Kinew told reporters during a break in the meeting that Canada needs a relationship between First Nations and the government “that reflects who Indigenous people are as Canadians.” Carney said “moving beyond” the Indian Act could involve abolition or reform. But he said it would only happen in partnership with First Nations leadership. “The suggestion of reforming, potentially abolishing and fully modernizing governance, is that a process, co-developed, needs to be put in place, and the federal government is open to that process,” Carney said. Carney said the idea of abolishing or modernizing the Indian Act was discussed openly in the room. “Not everybody, but other participants raised the desirability. So it’s already starting from the right place in that it’s not the federal government deciding something should be done. It’s responding to a request,” Carney said. “I think this was the spirit of this meeting — certainly the spirit I took — the ability to sit down together and develop that co-development, gives me hope that we can we can finally move forward from this.” The Indian Act has been in effect since 1876 to govern First Nations status in Canada. It has been amended several times to reflect changes in how status is conferred. Assembly of First Nations National Chief Cindy Woodhouse Nepinak said there are some protections in the act for First Nations, and First Nations should be able to decide how to move forward. “Look, that’s a question that was just posed today in the room among First Nations. Some First Nations; others would be very reserved,” Woodhouse Nepinak. “But there is, you know, a diversity of First Nations from coast to coast to coast, where in every province and territory in this beautiful country that we all share. And that question is going to be up to them to decide.” Kinew said he feels the Indian Act should be abolished altogether. He held up his First Nations status card, which he said identifies him as an “Indian within the meaning of the Indian Act.” “It’s time to abolish the Indian Act,” Kinew said. “It’s long overdue that we have a relationship with Indigenous Peoples in Canada that reflects who we are as Canadians today.” Carney and most of the premiers sat down with chiefs from the Assembly of First Nations in Ottawa for a discussion Woodhouse Nepinak said is intended to help build prosperity for coming generations. Monday’s closed-door meeting is the first such gathering since the Kelowna Accord talks of 2005, which brought premiers and then-prime minister Paul Martin together with Indigenous leaders to discuss ways to close the socioeconomic gaps in Indigenous communities. The Kelowna agreement was not implemented after the Conservative government under former prime minister Stephen Harper took office just a few months later. This meeting comes as Carney’s government works to speed up major project approvals and development — efforts some First Nations chiefs say threaten their rights. Jeronimo Kataquapit, who was protesting the major projects push outside the meeting venue in Ottawa, chided the federal government and the Assembly of First Nations over the lack of youth representation at the meeting. “These major projects cannot move forward without our free, prior and informed consent, and it’s the youth that stand to be the most impacted by the decisions made today by all leadership, both Indigenous and non-Indigenous alike,” Kataquapit said from the sidewalk in front of the Diefenbaker Building. Protester Katisha Paul, an advocate for youth and women, questioned the Assembly of First Nations’ mandate to negotiate on First Nations’ behalf. “I’m not in that room today but I can imagine and speculate that the voices of our ancestors are not being heard, they’re not being voiced and they’re not being amplified because many of those elected band council chiefs have lost their ways,” Paul said. Tensions between Ottawa and First Nations spiked soon after Carney was elected in 2025 when his government passed legislation to create a new office tasked with streamlining major project developments and approving projects within one year. First Nations leaders warned the compressed timelines would interfere with their rights and lead to court challenges. Provincial governments have enacted similar legislation. But tensions are boiling over for a number of other reasons as well, including the lands claim process in British Columbia, the newly announced Pacific Link pipeline project in Alberta and development of the mineral-rich Ring of Fire in Ontario. In many cases, it’s youth who are pushing back on First Nations leaders, the premiers and prime minister. Carney said Monday it’s “sobering” to consider that this is the first meeting to bring together federal, provincial and First Nations leaders in two decades. “Our task is twofold. First is to work together to create opportunities for all our peoples, while building a country that is stronger, more sovereign and more independent,” he said. “And secondly, our task is to live our values fully of a fair and inclusive Canada.” While some First Nations are opposed to Carney’s development agenda and those of the provinces, others are open to the idea of increasing economic activity in their territories. Nisga’a Nation President Eva Clayton told reporters ahead of the meeting she supports Carney’s plans and that she and other modern treaty holders are at the meeting to support Canada. By Alessia Passafiume and Kyle Duggan With files from Nick Murray

item.title: Meghan Roach steps down as Roots CEO after go-private deal closes
item.description: Roots Corp. says Meghan Roach has stepped down as president and chief executive as its go-private transaction with Marquee Brands has closed.
item.dc:creator: The Canadian Press
item.content:encoded: TORONTO — Roots Corp. says Meghan Roach has stepped down as president and chief executive as its go-private transaction with Marquee Brands has closed. Roach has been in the CEO role since 2020 after first joining the company as interim chief financial officer in 2019.  The company says in a news release she will continue to serve in an advisory role to ensure a smooth leadership transition. The go-private transaction was announced in August at a price of $4.10 per share and passed a shareholder vote earlier this month with more than 99 per cent support. The company says Roots shares are now expected to be delisted “shortly” from the Toronto Stock Exchange.    Marquee Brands also manages the Martha Stewart, Laura Ashley and Roberto Cavalli labels and intends to expand Roots to other markets like Korea, India and Mexico. --- This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 26, 2026.
